title: Upsweep
subtitle: The Upsweep sound · South Pacific, 1991
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the remote deep Pacific Ocean in the early 1990s, cold steel-blue and grey water, deep underwater darkness and heavy overcast, melancholy and uncanny, one centred subject in the middle third of a vertical frame, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: The Pacific, nineteen ninety-one. When NOAA began listening on the Navy's submarine hydrophones, one sound was already there.
beats.img: Deep underwater in the open ocean, a single cylindrical hydrophone listening device hanging on a taut vertical cable, centred in the frame and clearly lit by a soft cool shaft of light from far above, fine particles drifting, deep blue-black water all around, vast and silent.

beats.vo: A long train of rising tones, each several seconds long. Loud enough to be recorded across the Pacific.
beats.img: An old early-1990s computer CRT monitor on a metal desk in a dark ocean-acoustics lab, centred in the frame, its screen glowing green with a spectrogram of a repeating row of bright rising diagonal streaks, no numbers, no letters, no text, faint reflections on the curved glass, dim room.

beats.vo: It became known as Upsweep. It seems to come in seasons, peaking in spring and autumn.
beats.img: A neat stack of 1990s magnetic data-tape reels on a grey metal desk, centred in the frame under a single warm desk lamp, blank unlabelled reels, a pair of headphones resting beside them, rain on a dark window behind, no people.

beats.vo: Its source lies, roughly, in the remote South Pacific, between New Zealand and South America. Too steady, researchers said, to be a whale.
beats.img: Seen from just above the water, an empty, endless South Pacific under heavy grey overcast, long dark swells, no land, no ship, no animal, a faint misty patch of pale light in the centre of the frame where the horizon dissolves, cold and remote.

beats.vo: It lies near signs of undersea volcanic activity. More than thirty years on, NOAA calls its origin unresolved.
beats.img: Deep underwater, a dark volcanic seamount rising from the seafloor in the centre of the frame, a faint dull-orange glow and thin streams of bubbles at its summit, vast blue-black water around it, the top half fading into darkness, unresolved.

facts.claim: The sound was already present when NOAA/PMEL began recording the US Navy's SOSUS hydrophones (built for submarine surveillance) in August 1991 (acquisition began 29 Aug 1991)
It consists of a long train of narrow-band upsweeping (rising) sounds of several seconds each; source level high enough to be recorded throughout the Pacific
Known as 'Upsweep'; appears seasonal, generally peaking in spring and fall (unclear whether source or propagation changes)
Source roughly located at 54°S 140°W, a remote region of the South Pacific between New Zealand and South America
Initially attributed to fin whales; researchers dismissed a biological source because the tone has too little variation

Located near inferred volcanic seismicity (volcanic origin suspected, not established); NOAA states the origin of the sound is unresolved — unchanged as of Nov 2026 (PMEL page live; Wikipedia last edited 31 Oct 2026, no identification; no 2024-2026 report of a source)
Overall source level has declined since 1991 (caption only; NOAA's 'still detectable' line dates from a page unchanged since at least 2014, so not used)
